title: *CS302 - GDB Answer*
text:
*CS302 - GDB Answer*

`My Choice: Option A – BCD`

I support Option A, BCD, for this smart fuel dispenser.

The main reason is the output device. The dispenser has to show the amount on a 7-segment display, which is decimal in nature. In BCD, each decimal digit is already stored as a separate 4-bit code, so each digit can be directly sent to a BCD-to-7-segment decoder without any extra conversion. This makes the display logic simple and low-cost.

The maximum amount is Rs. 9,999.99, i.e. 999999 paisa, which needs only 6 BCD digits = 24 bits. This is easily handled by BCD adders. Although BCD adders need correction when the sum exceeds 9 by adding 6, this small extra logic is much cheaper than a large binary-to-BCD converter required in Option B.

In Option B, the amount is stored as pure binary. Binary adders are faster and use less hardware for calculation, but before display, the whole 20-bit binary number must be converted to decimal. That converter increases cost, complexity and delay, which is not suitable for a low-cost dispenser.

QR-code payment also deals with decimal amounts in paisa, so keeping the amount in decimal form from calculation to display reduces chances of conversion error and makes billing accurate.

Therefore, for low cost, simple display interfacing and accurate decimal billing, BCD is the better choice for this design.
